## Abstract

Glycolysis activation plays a critical role in sustaining the proinflammatory phenotype of macrophages, which is key to initiating and advancing liver fibrosis. However, the underlying mechanisms that trigger glycolytic activation and their contribution to inflammation remain poorly understood. In this study, we showed that inhibiting glycolysis markedly suppresses macrophage M1 polarization and alleviates liver inflammation and fibrosis, whereas enhancing glycolysis in hepatic macrophages produces the opposite effect. Additionally, our results demonstrated that glycolytic flux is necessary for activation of the STING/TBK1/IRF3 pathway. Moreover, STING activation was found to reciprocally stimulate glycolysis in macrophages. Mechanistically, we found that ATP generated through glycolysis promotes STING pathway activation and enhances the interferon-dependent immune response. Moreover, activation of IRF3, a downstream transcription factor of STING, upregulates HIF-1α transcription, further driving glycolysis. These findings uncover novel mechanistic links between STING signaling and glycolytic metabolism, emphasizing their coordinated role in promoting macrophage M1 polarization. Together, our data suggest that targeting the interaction between metabolic reprogramming and immune signaling offers an effective therapeutic approach for treating liver fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Keywords: glycolysis, innate immune response, liver fibrosis, macrophage

## Introduction

The increasing prevalence of chronic liver diseases presents a major global health challenge and contributes significantly to the worldwide economic burden1. Liver fibrosis (LF) is a critical intermediate stage in the progression of numerous chronic liver disorders toward cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and eventual liver failure. Evidence suggests that persistent, unresolved hepatic inflammation— primarily triggered by recurrent or chronic hepatocyte injury from diverse etiological factors—is central to the development of LF2, 3. However, due to the complex and multifaceted pathogenesis of LF, no

clinically approved antifibrotic therapies are currently available. Macrophages, as key players in innate immunity, are deeply implicated in the onset and progression of LF4. Upon stimulation by pathogen-associated molecular patterns or damage-associated molecular patterns, liver-resident macrophages (Kupffer cells) secrete a cascade of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines that drive immune cell recruitment and exacerbate hepatic inflammation5. In addition, transforming growth factor-β released by activated Kupffer cells stimulates

hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), promoting excessive collagen synthesis and fibrotic remodeling6. Importantly, macrophages undergo metabolic reprogramming in response to proinflammatory signals, characterized by a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis. This glycolytic reprogramming enables rapid ATP production, supporting the heightened biosynthetic and secretory demands of M1-type macrophages7. Given that the liver is the principal site of endogenous glucose production and glucose homeostasis8, it is particularly vulnerable to metabolic dysregulation. Nonetheless, the precise mechanisms by which augmented macrophage glycolysis contributes to hepatic inflammation remain insufficiently defined. The stimulator of interferon genes (STING) is a central mediator of innate immune responses and plays a vital role in maintaining hepatic immune balance by activating the NF-κB and IRF3 pathways, which in turn drive interferon (IFN) and cytokine production9. Recent studies have increasingly highlighted the involvement of STING signaling in various liver pathologies10, 11. Aberrant STING activation—induced by mitochondrial DNA leakage—has been reported in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), acute liver injury, and autoimmune hepatitis12, 13. Intriguingly, recent evidence suggests that glycolysis, independent of mitochondrial DNA leakage, also triggers STING pathway activation14. Despite these findings, the reciprocal interactions between enhanced glycolysis and STING signaling in macrophages during LF remain poorly defined. This study aims to elucidate the crostalk between macrophage glycolysis and STING signaling in the context of LF by focusing on the metabolic adaptability of macrophages. These insights may offer a conceptual framework for the development of targeted therapies to alleviate LF.

## Materials and Methods

Construction of myeloid-specific STINGknockout mice

We generated myeloid-specific STING knockout (STINGfl/fl/Lyz2-Cre, STINGM-KO) mice by crossing C57BL/6J background homozygous floxed STING (STINGfl/fl) mice (stock#031670; Jackson Lab) with Lyz2-Cre mice (C57BL/6J, stock# C001003; Cyagen), while STINGfl/fl mice served as controls. Genotyping for STINGM-KO mice was performed when the mice reached the age of 2 weeks using the following primers for PCR (sequence 5'–3'): Cre-Forward: CTTGGGCTGCCAGAATTTCTC; Cre-Reverse: CCCAGAAATGCCAGATTACG; LoxP- Forward: TTT TCA TCT GCC TTC CAG GT;

LoxP-Reverse: GCG CAC ACA CAC TAA AAA CTG.

Construction of a hepatic macrophage HK2- overexpression murine model

To generate a hepatic macrophage (MФs) HK2-overexpression murine model, we used AAV9 viral vectors to deliver the MФ-AAV9-F4/80-HK2 (F4/80) promoter, which drives the HK2 expression in hepatic MФs, into C57BL/6J mice via intrahepatic injection. The recombinant AAV9 was produced in HEK293T cells using pAAV-RC and pHelper, as described previously15, 16. The AAV9 viral vectors encoded HK2 under the control of the macrophage AAV9-F4/80-HK2 promoter. In addition, an empty vector under the regulation of the AAV9-F4/80 promoter (AAV9-F4/80-NC) was constructed concurrently. The viral titers for AAV9-F4/80-HK2 and AAV9-F4/80-NC were both 1.6 × 10¹² vector genomes (vg)/mL. Subsequently, 6 male C57BL/6J mice (age 6 weeks) were administered a 200 μL injection of either AAV9-F4/80-HK2 or AAV9-F4/ 80-NC vector, and the overexpression efficiency was confirmed 3 weeks after the injection.

Liver fibrosis model and treatment

The animal experiments conducted in this study received approval from the Ethics Committee of Wuhan University and were conducted as per the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Wild-type (WT) male C57BL/6 mice (weight: 18– 23 g, age: 6–8 weeks) were obtained from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu, China). All mice were housed under a standard pathogen-free laboratory environment with unrestricted access to water and chow diet, and were then randomly assigned to each group. The formal experiment was conducted after 7 days of acclimatization. All animals included in the study were subjected to the experimental procedures, and no animals were excluded from the analysis. WT, STINGfl/fl, and STINGM-KO mice (n = 6 in each group) were injected intraperitoneally (i.p.) with either a vehicle (normal saline) or 1% thioacetamide (TAA; Sigma, 163678) at a dose of 150 mg/kg body weight. The TAA treatment was administered from the third week for 12 consecutive weeks so as to induce liver fibrosis and assess the role of STING in this process. To examine the effect of glycolysis inhibition on established liver fibrosis, the experimental mice were injected i.p. with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG) at a dose of 1 g/kg/mouse every 3 days during the injection of TAA, in accordance with a previously described method17, 18. To examine the role of macrophage HK2 overexpression in liver fibrosis, the mice were first

Hepatic histopathological examination and serum biochemistry

After fixing the liver tissues with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) and embedding them in paraffin, 5-μm-thick slices were cut and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), Masson's trichrome, and Sirius Red for liver histopathological analyses. The serum levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were assessed using AST and ALT kits (ELK1778 and ELK1921, respectively; ELK Biotechnology) as per the manufacturer’s protocol.

Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) isolation and treatment

The bone marrow cells were isolated from STINGM/KO, STINGfl/fl, and WT mice (age: 6 weeks) and induced into macrophages (BMDMs). Briefly, after their euthanasia, the tibias and femurs of the mice were harvested and immersed in 75% ethanol for 5 min, and the bone marrow cells were flushed out using pre-cold PBS buffer. After centrifugation (1300 r.p.m. for 5 min at 4 °C), the pellets were resuspended in red blood cell lysis buffer (BL503A; Biosharp) for 5 min. The cells were then cultured in complete DMEM (Hyclone, USA) medium supplemented with 20 ng/mL M-CSF (315-02; PeproTech). The culture medium was refreshed on the third day, and the bone marrow cells were differentiated into macrophages on the 7th day at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator.

In vitro experimental design

The following experimental groups were established: Normal control (NC): BMDMs from WT, STINGfl/fl, and STINGM/KO mice were stored in complete medium (DMEM medium supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin‒streptomycin); (2) Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) group: for classical macrophage activation, BMDMs from WT, STINGfl/fl, and STINGM/KO mice were stimulated with LPS (L2880; Sigma) 100 ng/mL for 12 h; (3) 2-DG group: BMDMs from WT mice were cultured in a complete medium containing 2-DG (5 mM); (4) LPS+2-DG group: BMDMs from WT mice were pre-treated with 5 mM 2-DG for 12 h and then challenged with LPS (100 ng/mL) for another 12 h. (5) si-IRF3 group:

BMDMs were pre-transfected with small-interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting IRF3 or a negative control (si-NC) using Lipo3000 reagent (Invitrogen, USA) for 48 h, followed by LPS stimulation for 12 h. siRNA fragments targeting IRF3 were synthesized by Sangon Biotech (Wuhan, China), and the sequence was as follows (5’–3’): sense: GGUUCAGGAUCCCGUGGAA’; antisense: UUCCA CGGGAUCCUGAACC’.

Supplementation with ATP

The protocol was conducted in accordance with previously described methods14, 19. Briefly, BMDMs were treated with SLO (SAE0089, 800 ng/mL; Sigma) for 1 h, followed by 5 mM ATP (MCE, HY-B2176) for an additional 2 h. After treatment, BMDMs were exposed to LPS for 12 h. Moreover, to investigate the effects of glycolytic inhibition in vitro, BMDMs were pretreated with 2-DG before proceeding with the abovementioned experimental procedures. Finally, BMDMs were collected for WB analysis and ATP detection.

Lactate production assay

A Lactate Assay Kit (Cat# ab65331, Abcam) was applied to measure the L-lactate production in BMDMs and in mouse liver tissues. Then, 10 mg of the tissues or 2 x 106 macrophages were homogenized in 200 μL lactate assay buffer and centrifuged for 5 min at 12,800 rpm at 4°C. Then, the supernatants were collected into a clean tube, and lactate substrate mix and lactate enzyme mix were added into the tube to prepare the reaction mixture, which was then incubated for 30 min at the room temperature (RT), followed by determination of the lactate production by a microplate reader at OD 450 nm.

Flow cytometry analysis

To analyze macrophage polarization in vitro, BMDMs from among different groups were incubated with FITC-F4/80 and APC-Cy7-CD86 antibodies (123107 and 105029, respectively, Biolegend) at 4°C in the dark for 1 h, after washing and resuspending with cell-staining buffer, and the macrophages were subsequently analyzed by flow cytometry (Beckman, USA). All experiments were performed independently in triplicate, and the data were processed with FlowJo software.

Immunofluorescence (IF) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining

All primary and secondary antibodies used for IF and IHC are detailed in Supplementary Table 1. BMDM cell slides and 5-μm-thick liver sections were fixed with 4% PFA for 17 min and then blocked in 5%

Western blotting (WB) analysis

RIPA lysis buffer (Servicebio, China) was used for extracting proteins from the mice liver tissues or cultured BMDMs. The protein concentration was determined by BCA assay, and equal amounts were separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred onto PVDF membranes, and probed with primary antibodies overnight. The membranes were then incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary anti-mouse or anti-rabbit antibodies for 1 h. Signal detection was performed using the QuickChemi 5200 system, and the band intensities were quantified with ImageJ. All antibodies used in WB are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Quantitative real‑time PCR (RT-qPCR)

RNA was extracted from BMDMs and liver tissues using Trizol reagent (Invitrogen). After determining the concentration, 3 μg RNA was reverse-transcribed and amplified into cDNA by using the cDNA Synthesis Kit (RK20433; Abclonal). Subsequently, qPCR was conducted using the universal SYBR Green qPCR mix (RK21203; Abclonal). The primer sequences used for RT-qPCR are detailed in Supplementary Table 2. The relative mRNA expression of the target genes was quantified by the 2-ΔΔCT method, normalized to β-actin, and then analyzed with the Roche LightCycler® 480 system.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)

The BMDMs culture medium supernatants and mouse serum were collected for cytokine analysis. ELISA kits (Elabscience, China) were used to quantify the levels of TNF-α, IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, and IL-10 (Supplementary Table 3), and the assay was conducted following the manufacturer's protocols.

Extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) analysis

The ECAR of BMDMs was measured using the Seahorse XF Glycolytic Rate Assay Kit (103020-100; Agilent) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, the day before the experiment, the indicated BMDMs were plated at XF24 cell culture microplates (Agilent). The next day, the medium was exchanged with XF DMEM medium (103015-100; Agilent) and cultured in a CO2-free incubator at 37 °C for 1 h. Subsequently, the following substances were added at the designated timepoints: 10 mM glucose (glycolysis induction), 1 μM oligomycin (to maximize glycolysis), and 50 mM 2-DG (to inhibit glycolysis). The real-time ECAR data were automatically recorded by the XFe24 Extracellular Flux Analyzer (Agilent).

Dual-luciferase reporter assay

BMDMs were seeded into six-well plates. The potential binding site of IRF3 on the HIF- 1α promoter was predicted using the Animal Transcription Factors Database (AnimalTFDB4.0, https://guolab.wchscu.cn/AnimalTFDB4/#/). Dualluciferase reporter assay was performed to identify the targeting relationship between IRF3 and the HIF-1α promoter. Briefly, WT or mutant HIF-1α- promoter sequences (WT or Mut, respectively) were constructed into the pGL3 vector, whereas IRF3 was constructed into the pEnCMV-3xflag vector (Qinda Biol Co., LTD., China). Subsequently, the firefly luciferase plasmids pGL3-HIF-1α-WT and pGL3-HIF- 1α-Mut were co-transfected with pEnCMV-3xflag-NC (WT-IRF3), pEnCMV-3xflag-IRF3 (used for IRF3 overexpression in vitro, OE-IRF3), and pRL-TK renilla luciferase vector (internal reference) into BMDMs. After 48 h, a Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assay Kit (DL101-01; Vazyme) was applied to measure the firefly and renilla luciferase activities according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The luminescence signal was recorded by using a microplate reader (EnSight; PerkinElmer).

Targeted metabolomics analysis

Targeted metabolite profiling of BMDMs was performed using LC/MS-MS and conducted by Metware Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China). Briefly, BMDMs isolated from STINGM/KO and STINGfl/fl were stimulated without or with LPS, and the cells were collected and stored at -80 °C. Each group contained 4 duplicates. Next, the samples were dispersed with 800 μL of cold methanol/acetonitrile (1:1) and subsequently ultrasonicated for 20 min in an ice bath. Subsequently, the samples were centrifuged for 20 min (14000 xg, 4 °C) and the supernatants were harvested. Finally, the supernatants were analyzed by QTRAP™ 6500 LC-MS/MS System. Data were analyzed by Cluster 3.0 and the Java Treeview software. Differentiated metabolites were identified using Fold Change > 1.5, padj < 0.05 as the criteria.

Statistical Analyses

All statistical analyses were conducted using Student’s t-test or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Turkey’s test for comparison among groups. Data were expressed as the mean ±SEM and were analyzed by GraphPad Prism 9.5 software (GraphPad, USA). p < 0.05 indicated statistical significance.

## Results

Increased macrophage glycolysis in LF

To investigate the association between macrophage glycolysis and LF, we established a TAA-induced LF model in WT C57BL/6J mice. Additionally, BMDMs were generated from WT mice and polarized to the M1 phenotype by LPS stimulation. WB analysis was performed to assess the expression of key glycolytic rate-limiting enzymes, including hexokinase 2 (HK2), pyruvate kinase M2, and phosphofructokinase platelet type, both in vivo and in vitro. All three enzymes were significantly

upregulated in liver tissues from TAA-treated mice and in LPS-stimulated BMDMs compared with the NC group. Notably, HK2 exhibited the most pronounced increase in expression (Fig. 1A–D). IHC staining further confirmed the elevated HK2 expression in the livers of TAA-treated mice (Fig. 1E). We also evaluated HK2 expression in liver samples from patients with cirrhosis and NCs. IHC analysis revealed significantly greater HK2 positivity in liver sections from patients with cirrhosis than in those from NCs (Fig. 1H). Additionally, double IF staining for F4/80 and HK2 demonstrated elevated HK2 expression specifically in macrophages within both human and murine fibrotic liver tissues (Figs. 1F-G, 1I–J). To assess glycolytic flux in macrophages, ECAR was measured. The nonglycolytic acidification rate remained comparable between LPS-stimulated and control BMDMs. However, following glucose and oligomycin administration, the glycolytic acidification rate significantly increased in LPS-stimulated BMDMs, indicating enhanced glycolytic activity in M1-polarized macrophages upon LPS exposure (Figs. 1L–M). Furthermore, ATP and lactate levels were measured to assess glucose metabolism, and both were found to be elevated in activated BMDMs (Figs. 1K, N). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that increased macrophage glycolysis is a defining metabolic feature in LF.

2-DG treatment ameliorates TAA-induced mice LF

To examine the therapeutic potential of glycolysis inhibition, LF was induced in mice by repeated i.p. injections of TAA, with concurrent administration of the glycolysis inhibitor 2-DG throughout the treatment period (Fig. 2A). Histological analyses, including H&E, Masson's trichrome, and Sirius Red staining, showed marked hepatocyte swelling, inflammatory cell infiltration, extracellular matrix accumulation, and fibrotic changes in the livers of TAA-treated mice. In contrast, 2-DG-treated mice displayed substantial attenuation of these pathological features, along with reduced hepatic collagen deposition (Fig. 2B). Additionally, liver morphology in the 2-DG group was visibly improved compared with the TAA group. Serum biochemical analysis further revealed significantly lower ALT and AST levels in the 2-DG group (Figs. 2C, D). Since chronic liver inflammation contributes to fibrosis2, we next evaluated hepatic inflammation and fibrotic status using ELISA, reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), and WB analysis of serum and liver tissue. The TAA group exhibited

Inhibition of glycolysis suppresses STING signaling activation by reducing glycolytic ATP production

Given the pivotal role of the STING pathway in innate immunity and macrophage-mediated hepatic inflammation10, 21 and emerging evidence suggesting that glycolysis can activate STING signaling14 we therefore investigated whether 2-DG exerts its anti-inflammatory effects via modulation of this pathway. WB analysis revealed that both TAA exposure in vivo and LPS stimulation in vitro activated the STING signaling cascade, as shown by increased expression of STING, p-STING, phosphorylated TBK1 (p-TBK1), and phosphorylated IRF3 (p-IRF3), compared with the NC group (Figs. 4A–B and 4D–E). In contrast, 2-DG treatment markedly reduced the expression of these molecules in fibrotic liver tissue and LPS-stimulated BMDMs. IF staining further confirmed increased p-STING levels in liver macrophages after TAA administration, which were significantly diminished following 2-DG treatment (Fig. 4C). These results strongly support the role of glycolysis in driving STING pathway activation in macrophages. As ATP production is closely linked to glycolytic activity22, we next measured ATP levels in activated BMDMs. LPS stimulation significantly increased intracellular ATP, whereas 2-DG treatment sharply reduced ATP levels (Fig. 4F). To determine whether ATP depletion underlies the suppression of STING signaling, we delivered exogenous ATP to 2-DG-treated BMDMs using streptolysin-O. Notably, intracellular ATP was restored, and STING pathway activation resumed, confirming that glycolytic ATP is essential for maintaining STING signaling (Figs. 4G– H).

In summary, our data demonstrate that inhibition of glycolysis suppresses STING signaling in activated macrophages by reducing glycolytic ATP production, thereby mitigating hepatic inflammation.

Overexpression of HK2 in hepatic macrophages aggravates liver inflammation and fibrosis

To further investigate whether enhanced glycolysis in macrophages contributes to LF, we focused on HK2, a critical rate-limiting enzyme in the glycolytic pathway. HK2 was selectively overexpressed in hepatic macrophages via intrahepatic injection of AAV9 carrying an HK2-expressing vector under the control of the macrophage-specific F4/80 promoter (AAV9-F4/80-HK2). As a control, mice received an empty vector with the same macrophage-specific promoter (AAV9-F4/80-NC). Following viral delivery, mice injected with either AAV9-F4/80-HK2 or AAV9-F4/80-NC were subjected to the TAA-induced LF model (Fig. 5A). Myeloid STING deficiency suppresses glycolysis and M1 polarization in macrophage

To investigate the mechanistic impact of STING deletion on macrophage phenotype and metabolic status, we assessed macrophage polarization and the expression of downstream STING signaling components. STING knockout markedly reduced the TAA-induced increase in hepatic F4/80+CD86+ macrophages and lowered the expression of CD86, p-TBK1, and p-IRF3 (Figs. 8A–D). In parallel, BMDMs derived from STINGfl/fl and STINGM-KO mice were stimulated with or without LPS. WB revealed significantly lower levels of CD86, p-TBK1, and p-IRF3 in LPS-stimulated STINGM-KO BMDMs compared with STINGfl/fl controls (Figs. 8E–F). Flow cytometry, qPCR, and ELISA further confirmed that STING deficiency reduced the proportion of M1 macrophages and lowered the expression of inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IFN-β, IL-6, IL-1β, and IL-10 (Figs. 8G–J). Interestingly, during LPS stimulation, the culture medium of STINGM-KO BMDMs changed color more slowly than that of STINGfl/fl BMDMs, suggesting reduced acid production and altered metabolic activity (Fig. 9A). We hypothesized that STING deficiency impairs aerobic glycolysis. Indeed, under basal conditions, there were no significant differences in cellular ATP content or lactate production between STINGfl/fl and STINGM-KO BMDMs. However, following LPS exposure, ATP and lactate levels were significantly elevated in STINGfl/fl BMDMs but were markedly reduced in STINGM-KO BMDMs (Figs. 9B,

C). Seahorse metabolic analysis showed comparable basal ECAR between groups, but upon glucose and oligomycin addition during LPS stimulation, STINGM-KO BMDMs displayed significantly reduced ECAR, indicating impaired glycolytic capacity (Figs. 9E–F). Correspondingly, STING knockout reduced the TAA-induced increase in hepatic lactate levels and HK2 expression (Fig. 9D, 9H). IF staining further confirmed decreased HK2 expression in hepatic macrophages from the STING-deficient group following TAA exposure (Fig. S2A). To corroborate these findings, we performed central carbon metabolome profiling of BMDMs from STINGfl/fl and STINGM-KO mice, with or without LPS stimulation. Heatmap analysis revealed that several metabolites elevated by LPS were significantly suppressed in STING-deficient macrophages, even in the presence of LPS (Fig. 9G). Notably, the altered metabolites were closely linked to the glycolytic pathway and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, including dTMP, NAD, succinate, fumarate, pyruvate, and lactate. Collectively, these results confirm that STING is a critical driver of aerobic glycolysis and lactate production in macrophages, thereby promoting M1 polarization and inflammatory activation during LF.

IRF3-regulated HIF-1α contributes to the activation of glycolysis and STING signaling

The above findings suggest that glycolysis enhances STING signaling activation, whereas STING deficiency suppresses glycolytic activity. These observations imply the presence of a positive feedback loop between glycolysis and STING signaling. HIF-1α is a well-established transcription factor that drives glycolysis and promotes ATP production by upregulating key glycolytic enzymes, including HK223. Consistently, we observed that both TAA and LPS treatments increased HIF-1α and HK2 expression in liver tissues and BMDMs, respectively, whereas STING deficiency significantly reduced these inductions (Figs. 9H–I and Fig. S2B–C). Since STING activates type I IFN gene expression via phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of IRF324, we hypothesized that p-IRF3 transcriptionally regulates HIF-1α expression. Using Animal TFDB (https://guolab.wchscu.cn/AnimalTFDB4/#/), we predicted potential p-IRF3 binding sites in the HIF-1α-promoter region (Figs. 9J–K). Based on binding affinity scores, we selected the highestscoring binding site and constructed both WT (pGL3-HIF-1α-WT) and mutated (pGL3-HIF-1α-Mut; 5′→3′: “TCTCTCTCTTTTTTTCTTTT” mutated to “AGAGAGAGAAAAAAAGAAT”) promoter-

## Discussion

In this study, we demonstrated that glycolysis is significantly upregulated in both patients with cirrhosis and mouse models of LF, and that pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis markedly attenuates fibrosis progression. Mechanistically, we showed that glycolysis-derived ATP enhances activation of the STING/TBK1/IRF3 signaling pathway, triggering a type I IFN response and promoting M1 macrophage polarization. Moreover, STING activation upregulated HIF-1α, a key regulator of glycolysis, thereby forming a positive feedback loop that amplifies both metabolic and inflammatory responses. Collectively, these findings suggest that targeting dysregulated glucose metabolism in macrophages may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for managing cirrhosis. Chronic injury and unresolved inflammation are central to the initiation and progression of LF25, 26. Macrophages, as central effectors of innate immunity, demonstrate plasticity by shifting between M1 (proinflammatory) and M2 (anti-inflammatory) phenotypes in response to environmental cues. M1 macrophages contribute to fibrosis by activating HSCs, recruiting inflammatory cells, and promoting ECM deposition27. Importantly, M1 polarization is

accompanied by metabolic reprogramming from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis, enabling the production of ATP and biosynthetic intermediates required for inflammatory responses28. In addition to meeting metabolic demands, glycolysis generates signaling metabolites—such as lactate and succinate—that act as secondary messengers to promote inflammation. Lactate stabilizes HIF-1α, while succinate accumulation activates the NLRP3 inflammasome and promotes IL-1β secretion, amplifying immune responses29,30, 31. In line with these findings, our study showed that 2-DG effectively inhibited LPS-induced M1 polarization of BMDMs, decreased lactate production, and reduced inflammatory cytokine release. Furthermore, in vivo administration of 2-DG mitigated TAA-induced hepatic inflammation and fibrosis, evidenced by lower serum ALT/AST levels, reduced Ly6g+ neutrophil infiltration, and decreased numbers of M1 macrophages in the liver. These findings reinforce the concept that glycolysis plays a central role in driving macrophage-mediated inflammatory responses in fibrotic liver disease. Although HK2 is the initial rate-limiting enzyme in the glycolytic pathway, most previous studies on glycolytic enzymes in liver pathology have focused on pyruvate kinase M2 or GLUT1, often overlooking the role of HK2. In our study, however, HK2 emerged as a key regulator of macrophage glycolysis during liver fibrosis. Its overexpression in macrophages enhanced M1 polarization and increased neutrophil infiltration within the fibrotic liver, leading to exacerbated hepatic dysfunction. These results suggest that selectively targeting HK2-dependent glycolysis may offer a novel therapeutic approach to mitigate macrophage-driven inflammation and tissue damage in cirrhosis. Moreover, our study reveals a critical mechanistic link between glycolytic metabolism and innate immune activation. We demonstrate that ATP produced via glycolysis activates the STING/TBK1/IRF3 signaling axis, initiating type I interferon responses and reinforcing M1 macrophage polarization, consistent with recent findings in dendritic cells14. Notably, STING exhibits context-dependent functions in liver pathology. While its inhibition mitigates inflammation and lipid accumulation in lean NAFLD32, STING activation has been shown to suppress HBV replication and enhance antitumor immunity33, 34. However, most of these studies have focused on STING’s antiviral and immunomodulatory properties, with limited attention to its metabolic roles. Our findings extend this understanding by showing that 2-DG suppresses, whereas HK2 overexpression enhances, STING/

TBK1/IRF3 activation. Interestingly, STING deficiency in macrophages reduced glycolytic flux, ATP generation, and inflammatory activation, suggesting a bidirectional regulatory loop between metabolism and immune signaling. IRF3, a key downstream effector of STING, is increasingly recognized for its metabolic functions. It regulates adipocyte differentiation35, and its activity is elevated in patients with NAFLD. Hepatocyte-specific IRF3 knockdown improves insulin sensitivity and glycemic control in HFD-fed mice36. In addition, IRF3 drives hypoxia-induced renal fibrosis via upregulation of PFKFB3-dependent glycolysis37. However, its role in hepatic glycolytic regulation and macrophage polarization remains insufficiently characterized. HIF-1α is widely acknowledged as a central regulator of glycolysis23. Our experiments revealed that IRF3 directly binds to the HIF-1α promoter, promoting its transcription, while IRF3 silencing downregulates HIF-1α even in the presence of inflammatory stimulation. Since IRF3 activation is phosphorylation-dependent, our dual IF analysis showing coexpression and nuclear colocalization of p-IRF3 and HIF-1α in hepatic macrophages—both in vivo and in vitro—offers mechanistic insight into how STING signaling influences macrophage glycolytic reprogramming. Nevertheless, this study has limitations. While we identified macrophage glycolysis as a critical driver of LF, other glycolytic cell types, such as hepatocytes and HSCs, may also contribute to fibrogenesis. Although the AAV9 vector driven by the F4/80 promoter targets macrophages, potential transgene expression in other F4/80+ myeloid subsets cannot be excluded, possibly contributing to the observed effects. Furthermore, although STING deficiency led to decreased HIF-1α expression, further investigation is needed to establish whether HIF-1α is an indispensable downstream mediator of STING signaling in hepatic fibrosis.

## Conclusion

Our study demonstrates that TAA-induced LF is fueled by enhanced glycolysis in hepatic macrophages, primarily driven by HK2 upregulation. ATP generated through glycolysis activates the STING/TBK1/IRF3 pathway, promoting inflammation and upregulating HIF-1α, thereby establishing a positive feedback loop that intensifies glycolysis and inflammatory signaling. These findings offer novel mechanistic insight into how metabolic reprogramming amplifies innate immune responses and provide a compelling rationale for targeting glycolysis-STING signaling as a therapeutic strategy for LF and liver cirrhosis.

Hongtu Hu1,2,3, Zijing Zhu1,2,3, Lanlan Li 1,2,3, Jijia Hu1,2,3, Qian Yang1,2, Zhuan Peng1,2, Weiwei Li1,2, Xiaofei Cui1,2, Yanqin Fan1,2, Wenjie Chen1,2, Wei Liang 1,2 , Zhaowei Chen 1,2 & Guohua Ding 1,2

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major health issue, with podocyte injury with senescence playing a central role in glomerulosclerosis. This study investigates the link between glycolysis-derived serine metabolism and podocyte injury with senescence, focusing on the role of phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) in the regulation of L-serine synthesis and podocyte homeostasis. Using in vivo and in vitro models, we examined the effects of angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced metabolic dysregulation on serine metabolism and its impact on podocyte function. The results demonstrate that Ang II downregulates PGK1 expression through the transcription factor FOXA1, leading to reduced L-serine biosynthesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and increased cellular senescence in podocytes. Supplementing with L-serine or enhancing PGK1 expression in podocytes alleviated these pathological changes, restored mitochondrial function, and reduced senescence-associated phenotypes in CKD mouse models. Moreover, PGK1 was found to interact with keratin, type II cytoskeletal 1 (KRT1), stabilizing the cytoskeletal integrity of podocytes. These ﬁndings identify a novel metabolic pathway linking glycolysis, serine metabolism, and podocyte injury with senescence, suggesting that targeting the PGK1-serine axis may offer therapeutic potential for slowing podocyte senescence and CKD progression.

Podocytes are crucial components of the glomerular ﬁltration barrier, and their terminally differentiated nature makes them particularly vulnerable to injury. Podocyte injury is closely associated with the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD), driven by various glomerular disorders, including hypertensive nephropathy (HN) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD)1,2. Podocyte injury triggers a cellular senescence program, resulting in a state of long-term non-proliferative cells, which ultimately leads to podocyte senescence3. Notably, podocyte senescence is a hallmark of glomerulosclerosis, as senescent podocytes contribute signiﬁcantly to the deterioration of the ﬁltration

barrier, leading to proteinuria4. Since podocytes can not regenerate, the accumulation of senescent podocytes accelerates kidney function decline5. Previous studies have identiﬁed the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) activation, particularly angiotensin II (Ang II), as a critical factor in glomerular disease progression6. However, the direct contribution of Ang II to podocyte injury with senescence and the underlying mechanisms remains to be elucidated. pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) has been shown to further disrupts podocyte function7–9.While the partial restoration of glycolytic ﬂux through PKM2 activation alleviates podocyte injury, a complete reversal of Ang II-induced podocyte injury remains unachieved, suggesting that additional metabolic pathways contribute to disease progression10. Recent study has highlighted the role of glycolytic intermediates in regulating essential cellular functions, such as nucleotide, lipid, and amino acid syntheses11. Among these, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PG), an intermediate in glycolysis, serves as a precursor for L-serine synthesis. L-serine is pivotal in maintaining redox balance, supporting nucleotide synthesis, and modulating sphingolipid metabolism12. Notably, the kidneys are a primary organ for L-serine production, particularly during fasting13. However, the relationship between disturbed L-serine metabolism and podocyte injury and cellular senescence remains poorly understood. Phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) plays a crucial role in glycolysis by catalyzing the conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) to 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PG), which serves as the immediate precursor for serine biosynthesis. This effect occurs independent of the activity of other serine biosynthetic enzymes, such as phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH) and phosphoserine aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1), suggesting that PGK1 plays a central role in serine metabolism14,15. Despite this, the role of PGK1 in Ang II-induced podocyte senescence and glomerulosclerosis has not been fully elucidated. On the other hand, the precise mechanism by which PGK1- induced L-serine metabolism contributes to podocyte damage remains to be elucidated. It has been hypothesized that L-serine may playa role in sphingolipid production as substrates16. Sphingolipids are the most abundant lipids other than cholesterol in the podocyte lipid composition, and altered sphingolipid metabolism in podocytes promotes glomerular disease17. Furthermore, recent studies have demonstrated that altered L-serine metabolism contributes to the generation of deoxysphingolipids by serine palmitoyl-transferase (SPT)18. In addition, deoxysphingolipids have been shown to contribute to actin cytoskeleton derangement as well as cellular senescence neuronal cell19. However, the potential of Ang II-induced L-serine metabolism in podocytes to induce podocyte damage and cellular senescence by affecting deoxysphingolipid production remains to be elucidated. In the present study, we aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms in which PGK1-mediated serine metabolism contribute to Ang II-induced podocyte injury and cellular senescence. Additionally, we set out to determine whether L-serine supplementation or reinstatement of PGK1 expression can lessen renal injury in CKD mouse models, thereby presenting a therapeutic strategy to slow kidney senescence and curb CKD progression.

Results Ang II-induced serine deﬁciency, podocyte injury and cellular senescence Our previous studies have demonstrated that podocytes primarily rely on glycolysis for energy production, particularly in the foot process8. Activation of the RAS results in the inhibition of PKM2, a key glycolytic enzyme in podocytes, reducing glycolytic ﬂux. This metabolic disruption causes podocyte energy deﬁciencies, triggering actin cytoskeleton derangement and apoptosis. To further investigate the role of PKM2-mediated glycolysis in podocyte function, we measured the extracellular acidiﬁcation rate (ECAR) in podocytes under various interventions. Ang II stimulation signiﬁcantly decreased glycolytic ﬂux in podocytes. This effect was reversed by overexpression of PKM2 (Fig. 1A). Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) exert nephroprotective effects by inhibiting Ang II6. The results showed that ARB administration signiﬁcantly restored PKM2 expression in podocytes derived from patients with hypertensive nephropathy (HN) (Fig. 1B). However, ARBs

failed to fully restore synaptopodin (SYNPO) expression, indicating that Ang II-induced glycolytic disturbances may contribute to podocyte injury through additional pathways. Further RNA-seq analysis of HN patient kidney samples (GEO ID: GSE166239) revealed alterations in the amino acid biogenesis pathway (Fig. 1C), suggesting that disrupted amino acid metabolism plays a role in podocyte injury. Metabolomics analysis of podocytes subjected to Ang II, high glucose, or Adriamycin revealed signiﬁcant reductions in serine levels under all administration (Fig. 1D–F), highlighting serine as a key metabolite in podocyte dysfunction. We next examined the potential protective effects of serine supplementation in mitigating Ang II-induced podocyte injury. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) demonstrated that serine supplementation alleviated Ang II-induced mitochondrial damage in mouse podocytes (MPC-5) and human podocytes (HPC), reversing mitochondrial swelling and cristae breakage (Fig. 1G and Supplementary Fig. 1A). Flow cytometry showed that serine supplementation restored mitochondrial number and membrane potential in both MPC- 5 and HPC (Fig. 1H, I and Supplementary Fig. 1B, C). Additionally, serine supplementation improved mitochondrial function, as evidenced by increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP production in both cell lines (Fig. 1J and Supplementary Fig. 1D, E). Serine also reversed actin cytoskeleton derangement and lipid accumulation, as demonstrated by phalloidin and Oil Red O (ORO) staining in MPC-5 and HPC (Fig. 1K, L and Supplementary Fig. 1F–H). These ﬁndings suggest that serine supplementation improves mitochondrial function and cellular structure, mitigating Ang II-induced podocyte senescence. Senescence-associated β-galactosidase (β-Gal) staining revealed a dose-dependent reduction in cellular senescence following serine supplementation (Fig. 1M and Supplementary Fig. 1I, J). Serine also decreased the secretion of pro-inﬂammatory cytokines associated with the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), including IL-1β and IL-6 (Fig. 1N, O and Supplementary Fig. 1K, L), and reduced the expression of the DNA damage marker 8-hydroxy-2’-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) and the cell cycle regulator p21 (Supplementary Fig. 1M, N). To further investigate the role of non-essential amino acids in podocyte senescence and function, given that previous metabolomics studies identiﬁed a reduction in proline among non-essential amino acids, we further measured changes in proline levels under various interventions (Fig. 1F). The results indicated that proline levels in MPC-5 cells were also decreased under various interventions (Supplementary Fig. 1O). To further compare the effects of proline and serine on podocyte senescence and function, we treated MPC-5 cells with Ang II in the presence of serine or proline. β-Gal staining results indicated that both proline and serine could alleviate Ang II-induced podocyte senescence, with serine showing a more signiﬁcant effect (Supplementary Fig. 1P). Additionally, phalloidin staining results indicated that proline treatment was ineffective in alleviating actin cytoskeleton derangement in MPC-5, whereas serine treatment was effective (Supplementary Fig. 1P). These results indicate that serine supplementation attenuates Ang II-induced mitochondria dysfunction, actin cytoskeleton derangement, lipid accumulation, and cellular senescence in podocytes.

Serine regulates the production of deoxysphingolipids in podocytes via the PI3K/AKT pathway To explore the mechanisms underlying serine’s protective effects, we cultured podocytes in a serine-deﬁcient medium and treated with Ang II. TEM, OCR, and phalloidin staining revealed that serine deﬁciency exacerbated Ang II-induced structural damage and impairing function in mitochondria as well as worsening actin cytoskeleton derangement (Fig. 2A–C and Supplementary Fig. 2A). To further investigate the metabolic effects of serine deﬁciency, we performed untargeted metabolomics analysis, revealing a marked alteration in metabolic proﬁles across the different treatment groups (Fig. 2E). Hierarchical clustering analysis (HCA) identiﬁed 736 signiﬁcantly altered metabolites, with lipids representing the majority of these changes (Supplementary Fig. 2F). KEGG analysis revealed that the sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway was particularly enriched in the serine-deﬁcient group, with signiﬁcant increases in deoxysphingolipid content, such as dihydroceramide (DeoxyDHCer) and deoxy-ceramide (DeoxyCer) and 1-deoxysphinganine (DeoxySA), with the highest levels of DeoxyDHCer and DeoxyCer. And this result was observed in both the serine-deﬁcient group and Ang II-treated podocytes (Fig. 2G–I and Supplementary Fig. 2G). Notably, deoxysphingolipids exacerbated actin cytoskeleton derangement and cellular senescence in a dosedependent manner, reversing the protective effects of serine (Fig. 2J and Supplementary Fig. 2H–K). Typically, deoxysphingolipids is synthesized by SPT20. By using myriocin21 to inhibit SPT expression, cellular senescence in HPC and MPC was signiﬁcantly alleviated, and the expression of p21 and 8-OHdG as well as SASP was reduced (Supplementary Fig. 2L–U). In addition, further RNA-seq analysis identiﬁed signiﬁcant changes in oxidative phosphorylation and the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in response to serine deﬁciency (Fig. 2K, L). Furthermore, the correlation analysis of the untargeted metabolomics and RNA-seq demonstrated that the PI3K/AKT pathway was most signiﬁcantly altered in serine deﬁciency (Fig. 2M). It has been previously reported that certain amino acids are capable of binding to PI3K, thereby regulating PI3K phosphorylation22. It was therefore postulated that serine may regulate PI3K phosphorylation by binding to PI3K and thus regulating PI3K phosphorylation. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiments conﬁrmed that serine directly binds to PI3K and regulates phosphorylation (Fig. 2N and Supplementary Fig. 3A). Molecular docking experiments conﬁrmed that serine directly binds to the Thr462 site of PI3K (Fig. 2O). The SPR results showed that the mutation of the T462 site of PI3K signiﬁcantly reduced the binding of PI3K to serine. In addition, PI3K activity measurements showed that serine stimulated PI3K activity by 1.8 times, while the mutation of the T462 site had no such effect (Supplementary Fig. 3B, C). To further investigate the relationship between the PI3K/AKT pathway and PGK1 and serine, we ﬁrst used CRISPR/Cas9 technology to knockout PGK1 in MPC-5 cells. Given the lethality of PGK1-/- cells, we generated PGK1+/-

cells to facilitate analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3D). Western blot analyses conﬁrmed the reduction of PGK1 protein levels in MPC-5 cells (Supplementary Fig. 3E). We further complemented PI3K-WT and PI3K- T462A overexpression plasmids in PGK1+/- cells and treated them with serine or PI3K inhibitor (Wortmannin)23. PIP3/PIP2 measurement results indicate that the T462 site mutation of PI3K does not increase the enzyme activity of PI3K. Cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) and drug afﬁnity responsive target stability (DARTS) experiments further con- ﬁrm that the T462 site of PI3K is also critical for serine to enhance the stability of PI3K (Supplementary Fig. 3F–I). OCR and ATP measurements also showed that the mutation of the T462 site of PI3K reversed the upregulation of serine on mitochondrial function (Supplementary Fig. 3J, K). Additionally, the accumulation of deoxysphingolipids due to serine deﬁciency was mitigated by treatment with the PI3K agonist 740Y-P24, which alleviated actin cytoskeleton derangement and cellular senescence in podocytes (Fig. 2P, Q and Supplementary Fig. 3O–Q). These results demonstrate that serine regulates deoxysphingolipid metabolism in podocytes via the PI3K/AKT pathway.

PGK1 expression is downregulated in Ang II-induced podocyte injury Next, we conducted a more in-depth analysis of the de novo serine synthesis pathway. As previously mentioned, PGK1, PHGDH, and PSAT1

have been identiﬁed as pivotal rate-limiting enzymes (Fig. 3A). In order to ascertain the functions of these enzymes, we employed a short hairpin RNA (shRNA) approach to knockdown their expression in MPC- 5 cells. For this enzyme screen, each gene was silenced individually using shRNA (single-gene knockdown) rather than in combination. The results demonstrated that the knockdown of PGK1 or PHGDH had a signiﬁcant impact on serine production, but the knockdown of PGK1 signiﬁcantly decreased ATP production and podocyte senescence. Consequently, the subsequent investigations were concentrated on the function of PGK1 (Fig. 3B–D). Immunoﬂuorescence and Western blot analyses revealed that Ang II treatment downregulated PGK1 protein levels in both primary podocytes and cell lines (MPC-5 and HPC), which was accompanied by a reduction in PGK1 mRNA expression (Fig. 3E–G and Supplementary Fig. 4A–F). Additionally, analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data from patients with HN conﬁrmed that PGK1 expression was signiﬁcantly decreased in podocytes, correlating with age-related changes in serine metabolic pathways (Fig. 3H–M). Furthermore, the down-regulation of PGK1 expression was further conﬁrmed by immunoﬂuorescence and immunohistochemical staining of patient kidney tissue with HN (Fig. 3N and Supplementary Fig. 4G, H). Further clinical correlation analysis demonstrated that lower PGK1 expression was associated with increased proteinuria and albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR), decreased estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate (eGFR), and poorer prognosis, suggesting that PGK1 plays a nephroprotective role in patients with HN (Fig. 3O–S and Table S2).

PGK1 regulates the PI3K/AKT pathway in podocytes and is associated with deoxysphingolipid accumulation and cellular senescence Given that PGK1 is involved in both serine metabolism and the tricarboxylic acid cycle, we performed isotope labeling using Dglucose-13C6 to assess the impact of PGK1 knockdown on serine metabolism and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates (Fig. 4A). PGK1 knockdown resulted in a signiﬁcant decrease in serine production and a reduction in pyruvate and TCA intermediates, including citrate (Fig. 4B–D). In addition, PGK1 knockdown also signiﬁcantly increased 1,3-BPG and reduced 3-PG contents (Fig. 4E, F). These data suggest that PGK1 participates in serine biosynthesis and plays a key regulatory role in the TCA cycle, enhancing mitochondrial respiration in podocytes. Further investigation revealed that PGK1 knockdown in MPC-5 cells led to mitochondrial structural damage, as observed by TEM, and functional impairment, as indicated by reduced OCR (Fig. 4G, H). Moreover, PGK1 knockdown exacerbated actin cytoskeleton derangement and podocyte senescence, as evidenced by increased β- Gal staining and upregulation of 8-OHdG and p21 expression (Fig. 4I, J and Supplementary Fig. 5A, B). These effects mirrored those observed with serine deﬁciency (Fig. 2C, D and Supplementary Fig. 2B, C). Untargeted metabolomics analysis of MPC-5 cells demonstrated signiﬁcant metabolic shifts in PGK1 knockdown cells, with 494 metabolites identiﬁed, the majority of which were lipids (Fig. 4K, L). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), KEGG pathway analysis and Western blot analyses revealed alterations in sphingolipid metabolism and the PI3K/ AKT pathway (Fig. 4M, N and Supplementary Fig. 5C–F). Furthermore, deoxysphingolipids were notably elevated in PGK1 knockdown cells (Fig. 4O). RNA-seq data further supported these ﬁndings, indicating signiﬁcant changes in metabolic and senescence-related pathways, particularly those involving the PI3K/AKT signaling axis (Fig. 4P–R). Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) further conﬁrmed that PGK1 knockdown impacts the PI3K/AKT pathway, which is associated with cellular senescence and p21 activation (Fig. 4S, T). These ﬁndings suggest that PGK1 regulates podocyte function through sphingolipid metabolism and the PI3K/AKT pathway.

Given the pivotal function of KRT1 in cytoskeleton maintenance and the established link between cytoskeleton and cellular senescence, we undertook a detailed investigation into the impact of KRT1 on cytoskeleton and podocyte senescence. Further ﬁndings revealed that KRT1 knockdown led to pronounced actin cytoskeleton derangement and a notable exacerbation of podocyte senescence, and this effect was not reversed by PGK1 overexpression (Fig. 5O–Q). Next, we further explored the dual enzymatic and non-enzymatic functions of PGK1. It has been reported that PGK1 exerts its enzymatic activity through the K13126 and T16827 sites, while protein-protein docking results indicate that PGK1 binds to KRT1 via the 200-360aa region. Therefore, we separately overexpressed PGK1-WT, PGK1-K131A, PGK1-T168A, and PGK1-Δ200-360 plasmids in PGK1+/- cells. Co-IP results showed that the deletion of the 200-360aa region of PGK1 signiﬁcantly reduced KRT1 expression, but mutations at the K131 and T168 sites had no obvious effect on KRT1 expression (Supplementary Fig. 6A). Serine content, OCR, and ATP measurement results indicated that serine production and mitochondrial function were signiﬁcantly inhibited after mutations at the K131 and T168 sites, but the Δ200-360 group showed almost no effect (Supplementary Fig. 6B–D). Additionally, β-Gal and phalloidin staining results (Supplementary Fig. 6E) further indicate that PGK1 catalytic activity is crucial for maintaining serine metabolism, mitochondrial function, and preventing podocyte senescence, while the PGK1-KRT1 interaction further regulates podocyte senescence by maintaining podocyte cytoskeletal integrity, representing an enzyme activity-independent mechanism.

Podocyte-speciﬁc overexpression of PGK1 attenuates podocyte injury with senescence in Ang II-induced mouse model To assess the in vivo role of PGK1, we generated a podocyte-speciﬁc PGK1 overexpression mouse model (PGK1podKI) by crossing PGK1ﬂoxed/

ﬂoxed mice with Podocin-Cre mice (Supplementary Fig. 7A, B). Western blot analyses conﬁrmed successful PGK1 overexpression in podocytes (Supplementary Fig. 7C). While PGK1podKI mice exhibited no signiﬁcant changes in basal renal function or pathology compared to controls, they showed signiﬁcant protection from Ang II-induced podocyte injury (Fig. 6A–E and Supplementary Fig. 7D). PGK1podKI mice exhibited improved mitochondrial respiration and enhanced mitochondrial function following Ang II treatment (Fig. 6F, G). Podocyte-speciﬁc PGK1 overexpression also attenuated podocyte senescence, including lipid and deoxysphingolipid accumulation, as well as markers of senescence such as p21 and 8-OHdG (Fig. 6H–J and Supplementary Fig. 7E–H). In addition, overexpression of PGK1

signiﬁcantly reduced 1,3-BPG and increased 3-PG contents (Fig. 6K, L). These ﬁndings were associated with activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway (Supplementary Fig. 7I, J). Moreover, the use of an AAV to rapidly increase PGK1 expression in PGK1ﬂoxed/ﬂoxed mice signiﬁcantly mitigated Ang II-induced podocyte senescence and glomerular pathology injury, conﬁrming that postnatal enhancement of PGK1 expression can effectively counteract podocyte senescence (Fig. 6M–R and Supplementary Fig. 7K). These results showed the potential of podocytespeciﬁc PGK1 overexpression as a therapeutic strategy to mitigate podocyte senescence.

Podocyte-speciﬁc knockout of PGK1 exacerbates podocyte senescence in Ang II-induced mouse model To further investigate the role of PGK1 in podocyte injury with senescence, we generated a podocyte-speciﬁc PGK1 knockout mouse model (PGK1podKO) (Supplementary Fig. 8A, B). Western blot analyses con- ﬁrmed successful PGK1 knockout in podocytes (Supplementary Fig. 8C). In contrast to PGK1podKI mice, PGK1podKO mice exhibited signiﬁcant exacerbation of Ang II-induced podocyte injury, characterized by worsened mitochondrial function and glomerular damage (Fig. 7A–E and Supplementary Fig. 8D). While mitochondrial respiration was not signiﬁcantly altered in PGK1podKO mice under baseline conditions, Ang II treatment exacerbated mitochondrial dysfunction (Fig. 7F, G). Furthermore, PGK1podKO mice showed enhanced podocyte senescence, including increased lipid and deoxysphingolipid accumulation, SASP activation, and elevated p21 and 8-OHdG expression (Fig. 7H–J and Supplementary Fig. 8E–I). In addition, knockout of PGK1 signiﬁcantly increased 1,3-BPG and reduced 3-PG contents (Fig. 7K, L). These ﬁndings were accompanied by inhibition of the PI3K/AKT pathway (Supplementary Fig. 8J). Additionally, using the speciﬁc PGK1 inhibitor Z57346765 exacerbated Ang II-induced podocyte senescence in normal mice, further supporting the role of PGK1 in glomerular homeostasis (Fig. 7M–R). These results demonstrate that podocytespeciﬁc PGK1 knockdown exacerbates podocyte injury with senescence, highlighting the critical role of PGK1 in maintaining glomerular function.

Serine supplementation attenuates Ang II-induced podocyte senescence in mouse models We further validated the protective effects of serine supplementation in vivo using an Ang II-induced mouse model (Supplementary Fig. 10A). We treated podocytes and mouse models with the same dose as in previous studies18, and serine supplementation restored intracellular L-serine levels to physiological ranges, with no detection of supraphysiological levels of serine in treated cells. Four weeks of serine supplementation signiﬁcantly improved renal function, as evidenced by reduced urinary ACR, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and serum creatinine (Cr) levels (Fig. 9A–E). Histological analysis, including HE staining, SYNPO staining, TEM and scanning electron microscope (SEM), revealed that serine supplementation improved glomerular architecture, including mesangial matrix expansion, foot process damage, and podocyte cytoarchitectural integrity (Fig. 9A–E and Supplementary Fig. 10B). Serine supplementation also increased mitochondrial

function in the mouse model and primary podocytes, as indicated by enhanced OCR and ATP levels (Fig. 9F, G and Supplementary Fig. 10C, D). Additionally, serine supplementation activated the PI3K/AKT pathway in primary podocytes (Fig. 9H and Supplementary Fig. 10E). Further investigations revealed that serine supplementation reduced markers of podocyte senescence, including the expression of p21 and 8-OHdG, and attenuated the accumulation of lipid and deoxysphingolipids (Fig. 9I–L and Supplementary Fig. 10F). These results suggest that serine supplementation may be beneﬁcial in attenuating Ang II-induced podocyte injury with senescence in animal models.

Discussion This study highlights the critical role of the PGK1-mediated serinedeoxysphingolipid pathway in regulating podocyte injury with senescence, particularly in Ang II-induced mouse models. We further demonstrate that PGK1 is signiﬁcantly inhibited in both patients with HN and Ang II-induced mouse models. Moreover, the present study shows that PGK1 overexpression in podocytes mitigates the effects of Ang II on podocyte injury with senescence, whereas its knockdown exacerbates podocyte senescence and glomerular pathological injury. Further mechanistic studies reveal that PGK1 governs the de novo synthesis of serine and regulates mitochondrial respiration in podocytes. Additionally, we ﬁnd that serine supplementation signiﬁcantly alleviates podocyte senescence and glomerular pathological injury in Ang II-induced and non-Ang II-induced CKD mouse models, with evidence of modulation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, deoxysphingolipids production, and podocyte injury with senescence. Furthermore, PGK1 was shown to maintain cytoskeletal integrity by binding to and stabilizing KRT1. Finally, FOXA1 emerged as a key regulator of PGK1 expression, providing a novel transcriptional mechanism in Ang IIinduced podocyte injury with senescence. The activation of the RAS by Ang II is a well-established factor in the progression of CKD and has been shown to exacerbate podocyte and glomerular injury. Being terminally differentiated, podocytes are particularly susceptible to Ang II-induced damage30,31. Our previous studies have conﬁrmed that Ang II induces apoptosis and cellular shedding in podocytes, but the onset of podocyte senescence appears to precede other forms of damage, as a key event in glomerular injury8,32,33. The present study provides evidence that podocyte

senescence is an early and signiﬁcant contributor to glomerular injury in patients with HN and animal models. These ﬁndings emphasize the critical role of podocyte senescence in glomerular pathological injury and disease progression. Cellular senescence is typically characterized by irreversible proliferative arrest and is triggered by various stressors, including DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inﬂammation34,35. Senescent cells exhibit altered chromatin structure, dysregulated gene expression, and the secretion of pro-inﬂammatory cytokines, collectively known as the SASP36,37. The present study conﬁrms that senescent podocytes exhibit elevated levels of DNA damage markers such as 8- OHdG, upregulation of p21, and impaired mitochondrial respiration. The SASP, including increased secretion of IL-1β and IL-6, was also observed in Ang II-treated podocytes, further contributing to renal aging and injury. These ﬁndings are consistent with the wellestablished role of senescence in tissue aging and suggest that targeting senescence could offer therapeutic beneﬁts in CKD. Serine, a non-essential amino acid, plays a pivotal role in numerous cellular processes, including energy metabolism, antioxidant defense, and protein synthesis12,38. It exists in two enantiomeric forms: L-serine, which is prevalent in most tissues, including the kidney, and D-serine, which is predominantly found in the brain16,39. The regulation of L-serine synthesis is crucial for maintaining cellular function, and disruptions in this pathway have been implicated in several metabolic disorders, including diabetic neuropathy, obesity, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis18,40. Recent large prospective cohort studies suggest that serine enantiomers may serve as sensitive indicators of kidney injury, potentially exerting an effect independent of etiology41. In type 2 diabetes, a untargeted/targeted ¹H-NMR detection panel identiﬁed the serine/creatinine ratio as an early biomarker capable of distinguishing early DKD from uncomplicated diabetes42. Pediatric data further show that the D/L-serine ratio is positively correlated with creatinine and cystatin-C, and is unaffected by growth or glucocorticoid therapy, supporting its application across the entire lifespan. Finally, reduced plasma L-serine levels are associated with cognitive decline and reduced eGFR in hemodialysis patients, suggesting a systemic impact of renal serine depletion in age-related CKD43. Overall, these human studies position the PGK1-serine axis as a common metabolic checkpoint for podocyte injury and CKD progression and highlight the translational potential of measuring circulating serine as a non-invasive biomarker for risk stratiﬁcation and monitoring treatment response. In this study, our ﬁndings extend this knowledge by demonstrating that Ang II-induced podocyte senescence is associated with reduced L-serine levels and that serine supplementation signiﬁcantly reverses these effects. One of the novel ﬁndings in this study is identifying deoxysphingolipids as key metabolites regulated by L-serine in podocytes. Sphingolipids are abundant in podocytes and have been linked to glomerular diseases44,45. Our metabolomics data show that L-serine deﬁciency leads to increased levels of deoxysphingolipids, which in turn promote podocyte senescence. This ﬁnding suggests a metabolic link between serine metabolism and sphingolipid production, which could contribute to the progression of podocyte senescence. In imbalanced serine metabolism, SPT mistakenly incorporates alanine or

glycine into the substrate, producing DeoxyDHCer and its dehydrogenated product, DeoxyCer, both of which lack the C1-hydroxy group20. These two types of “deoxyceramides” can not be further phosphorylated or degraded, leading to their accumulation within podocytes. Compared to conventional Cer/DHCer, DeoxyDHCer and DeoxyCer are more likely to insert into the outer mitochondrial membrane and inhibit complex III, triggering ROS bursts and loss of membrane potential46. Simultaneously, their lack of polar head groups increases lipid raft rigidity, disrupting the actin-integrin signaling essential for foot processes. Furthermore, following SPT inhibition or serine supplementation, DeoxyDHCer/ DeoxyCer levels decrease most signiﬁcantly, with corresponding improvements in mitochondrial function and structural integrity occurring ﬁrst. Overall, DeoxyDHCer triggers aging through the mitochondrial-ROS-DDR pathway, while DeoxyCer maintains the aging phenotype and ampliﬁes structural damage. Together, they form the core of serine depletion-driven podocytes senescence. Moreover, we have demonstrated that serine regulates the PI3K/ AKT pathway, crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis49,50. Inhibition of this pathway exacerbates deoxysphingolipids accumulation and podocyte senescence, while serine supplementation restores the PI3K/AKT signaling axis and alleviates these effects. This highlights a potential therapeutic target in the serine-PI3K/AKT-deoxy sphingolipid axis for mitigating podocyte senescence. PGK1, a key enzyme in glycolysis, plays a dual role in energy metabolism and serine biosynthesis51. Although much attention has been focused on the role of PHGDH in L-serine synthesis52, recent studies have shown that altered glycolytic ﬂux, rather than changes in PHGDH expression, is the primary cause of reduced serine production in disease states53. The present study demonstrates that PGK1 is essential for maintaining serine synthesis and mitochondrial function in podocytes. Knockdown of PGK1 leads to decreased ATP production, reduced serine synthesis, and increased accumulation of deoxysphingolipids, which exacerbates podocyte senescence and glomerular pathological injury. These ﬁndings implicate PGK1 as an important component of a coordinated regulatory network that integrates glycolysis with serine biosynthesis and cellular stress responses. Additionally, we have demonstrated that PGK1 interacts with KRT1, a key regulator of cytoskeletal integrity54. PGK1 stabilizes KRT1 protein, preventing its degradation and maintaining the structural integrity of podocytes. This interaction offers a new insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying podocyte injury and podocyte senescence. Moreover, we identiﬁed FOXA1 as a key transcription factor regulating PGK1 expression. FOXA1 is downregulated in response to Ang II stimulation, reducing PGK1 expression and exacerbating podocyte senescence. Rescue experiments indicate protective effects of FOXA1 are only partially dependent on PGK1, suggesting that additional PGK1-independent targets/pathways may be involved. Despite these promising ﬁndings, several limitations of the study warrant consideration. First, most of our experiments were conducted in animal models and in vitro, which may not fully replicate the complex pathophysiology of human kidney disease. Future studies incorporating clinical samples and larger patient cohorts will be necessary to validate the observed effects. Second, most untargeted metabolomics data are inferred annotations (MSI 2/3), and statistical associations alone cannot establish causality. Third, while serine supplementation shows potential, its long-term safety and effects on other organs remain unclear. Further clinical trials are required to assess the broader applicability of serine-based therapies for podocyte senescence and other kidney diseases, including DKD and hereditary nephropathies. In conclusion, our ﬁndings underscore the importance of the PGK1- regulated serine-deoxysphingolipid pathway in Ang II-induced podocyte injury and cellular senescence. PGK1-derived serine metabolism is key to maintaining podocyte function and glomerular homeostasis. These results provide a compelling scientiﬁc foundation for developing serine supplementation or PGK1 activation as a potential therapeutic strategy for CKD. Future studies focused on the regulatory mechanisms of PGK1 and its interaction with FOXA1 may offer new avenues for the treatment of podocyte senescence and kidney disease.

Methods Collection of human kidney biopsy specimens and clinical indicators Control kidney samples were obtained from non-diseased areas adjacent to cancerous tissue, whereas hypertensive nephropathy (HN) kidney samples were collected from patients with pathological changes consistent with HN, as conﬁrmed by renal biopsy. All patients were informed of the usage of their urine and blood, and written informed consent was obtained. No sex or gender analysis was performed due to the low sample size. Detailed clinical characteristics of the patients are provided in Tables S1 and S2. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University (Approval number: WDRY2023-K040).

Mouse studies Mice were housed in a pathogen-free environment with controlled humidity (40-70%), temperature (20 °C-25 °C), and a 12-hour light/dark cycle. They had unrestricted access to food and water. After the treatment period, all mice were humanely euthanized via intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (200 mg/kg), and kidney samples were collected for subsequent analysis. The entire experimental procedure was blinded, and the Ethical Committee approved all animal experiments for the Experimental Use of Animals at Renmin Hospital, Wuhan University (Approval number: WDRM-20250602).

Establishment and treatment of Ang II-induced mouse model and non-Ang II-induced CKD mouse models Male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old, 20–25 g) were obtained from Cyagen Biosciences Co. To induce hypertension and renal injury, mice were implanted with an osmotic micropump delivering Ang II (700 ng/ kg/min) for 28 days8. Control mice received an equal volume of saline via osmotic pumps. In the Adriamycin (ADR)-induced mouse model, Male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old, 20–25 g) were injected with ADR (20 mg/kg) intravenously in the tail55. In the DKD mouse model, 16- week-old male type 2 diabetic db/db mice and genetic control db/m mice were obtained from the Cytogenes Biosciences Co.56. After the treatment period, mice were euthanized, and kidneys were harvested for further analysis.

L-serine treatment L-serine (Bio Basic Inc, SB1479) was dissolved in sterile water and administered to mice via oral gavage at a dose of 280 mg/day. Treatment began on day 0 and continued for 28 consecutive days. The treatment regimen was chosen based on previous study57 and aimed to achieve a therapeutic dose that would provide measurable effects on podocyte function and mitochondrial health.

Generation and treatment of PGK1podKI and PGK1podKO mice Podocyte-speciﬁc overexpression of PGK1 (PGK1podKI) was achieved by crossing PGK1ﬂoxed/ﬂoxed mice (C57BL/6; Cyagen Biosciences, China) with Podocin-Cre mice (C57BL/6; Cyagen Biosciences, China). For podocyte-speciﬁc PGK1 knockout (PGK1podKO), PGK1ﬂoxed/ﬂoxed mice were crossed with Cre-expressing mice (C57BL/6). Pure ﬂoxed mice from the same litter without Cre expression served as controls (PGK1ctrl). Male PGK1podKI and PGK1podKO mice (6–8 weeks old, 20–25 g) were randomly assigned to the experimental groups.

Intrarenal adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery To investigate the effects of FOXA1 on PGK1 regulation in vivo, FOXA1 overexpression was induced by intrarenal injection of adenoassociated virus (AAV) vectors. AAV-nphs1-FOXA1 (AAV-FOXA1) and control AAV-nphs1-null (AAV-ctrl) (Hanbio Co., Ltd., China) were administered to mice via in situ renal injections at six points, four weeks before osmotic pump implantation.

Glomerular isolation Mouse glomeruli were isolated following the method described previously8. Kidneys were minced into small pieces (~1 mm3) and digested in a collagenase II, protease E, and deoxyribonuclease I solution for 30 minutes at 37 °C with gentle agitation. After digestion, the tissue was ﬁltered through 100 µm, 70 µm, and 40 µm cell sieves, and glomeruli were collected by rinsing the 40 µm sieve. Glomeruli were centrifuged at 1500 rpm for 5 minutes at 4 °C and resuspended in 5 ml of culture medium.

Podocyte culture and treatment Mouse podocytes (MPC-5) were obtained from BNCC (China) and cultured in DMEM-H medium (Hyclone, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Life-iLab, China) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Biosharp, China). The cells were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO₂. A conditioned medium (serine-free ECM) was purchased from ScienCell. Conditioned immortalized human podocytes (HPC) were provided by Professor Moin A. Saleem (Southmead Hospital, Bristol, UK). Primary human podocytes were isolated as described in previous protocols8. HPC and primary human podocytes were cultured at 33 °C in RPMI 1640 (HyClone, USA) medium supplemented with 10% heatinactivated fetal bovine serum (Gibco, USA), 100 U/mL penicillinstreptomycin (Invitrogen, USA), and 1× insulin-transferrin-selenium (ITS; Invitrogen, USA). For differentiation, cells were incubated in an ITS-free medium at 37 °C for 10-14 days before treatment. Podocytes were treated with Ang II (Sigma, USA) at 10-6M for 24 hours. Cycloheximide (CHX; TargetMol, China) was used at 20 µM for 12 hours, and MG132 (TargetMol, China) at 10 µM for 8 hours. L-serine (Sigma, USA) was administered at 600 µM for 48 hours. Deoxysphingolipids (Sigma, USA) were used at 5 µM for 24 hours, and 740Y-P (TargetMol, China) at 20 µM for 24 hours.

Construction of the PGK1+/- cell line Cyagen Biosciences Co., Ltd. (China) generated the PGK1+/- cell line using CRISPR/Cas9 technology. This process included designing and synthesizing sgRNA targeting PGK1, transfecting cells, monoclonal screening, and veriﬁcation through sequencing.

Metabolic cage analysis Metabolic phenotyping was performed using the PhenoMaster system (TSE Systems) for indirect calorimetry analysis in mice. Each mouse was housed individually during the experiment. After a 2–3 days acclimatization period, key metabolic parameters such as food intake, water intake, oxygen consumption (VO2), carbon dioxide production (VCO2), respiratory exchange ratio (RER), and total activity were continuously monitored over a minimum of one week, with measurements recorded hourly.

Renal function parameter measurement Before euthanasia, blood samples were collected via orbital sinus puncture and analyzed using an automated biochemical analyzer (Beckman, USA) to measure serum creatinine (Cr) and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels. Mice were individually housed in metabolic cages for 24 hours to collect urine samples. Urine was centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 10 minutes at 4 °C, and the supernatant was used for subsequent analyses. The urinary albumin concentration was determined using an ELISA kit (Abcam, USA). The urinary albumin-tocreatinine ratio (ACR) was calculated by dividing the urinary albumin concentration by the serum creatinine concentration.

IL-1β and IL-6 content measurement Levels of IL-1β and IL-6 were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits in isolated mouse glomeruli, patient serum, and treated podocyte cultures.

Cell transfection Short hairpin RNAs (shRNA) targeting PGK1, KRT1, and FOXA1 (sh- PGK1, sh-KRT1, sh-FOXA1) and a full-length PGK1 expression plasmid (OE-PGK1) were used to transfect MPC-5 cells with HiPerFect Transfection Reagent (Qiagen, Germany) and X-tremeGENE HP DNA Transfection Reagent (Roche, Switzerland). For the enzyme-screen experiment, shRNAs targeting PGK1, PHGDH, and PSAT1 were used individually (two non-overlapping shRNA sequences per gene). Knockdown efﬁciency was veriﬁed by RT-PCR and Western blot. The same transfection method was used for HPC cells. Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors carrying the PGK1 gene (AAV-PGK1) or a control vector (AAV-ctrl) were transfected into MPC-5 cells (Hanbio Co. Ltd., China). Experiments were conducted 24 hours after transfection.

Histological and immunohistochemical (IHC) analyses Kidney tissues from both mice and patients were ﬁxed, dehydrated, and embedded in parafﬁn. Sections were dewaxed, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval. For histological analysis, hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining was performed to evaluate renal tissue pathology. Glomerular mesangial matrix expansion was quantiﬁed by measuring the area in 30 randomly selected, non-overlapping ﬁelds per group (ﬁve ﬁelds per section). For IHC, sections were incubated with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 1 hour at room temperature, followed by incubation with primary antibodies against 8-OHdG, PGK1, and FOXA1 (all from Genetex, USA) at 4 °C overnight. Immunoreactivity was detected using HRP-coupled secondary antibodies, with diaminobenzidine as a substrate. Images were captured using an Olympus upright microscope.

Immunoﬂuorescence assay Kidney sections and podocyte membrane samples were subjected to the same preparation as for IHC. After ﬁxing the podocyte membranes with 5% BSA, sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies (FOXA1, 8-OHdG, PGK1, p21, GLB1, Synaptopodin, WT1, KRT1) from Abcam (USA) and Bosterbio (China). Secondary antibodies conjugated to HRP were applied for 1 hour at room temperature, followed by nuclear staining with DAPI. Images were captured using a confocal microscope (Olympus, Japan). Average ﬂuorescence intensity was quantiﬁed in 15 randomly selected, non-overlapping ﬁelds per group (ﬁve ﬁelds per section).

ATP measurement According to the manufacturer’s instructions, ATP levels in podocytes were measured using an ATP assay kit (Beyotime, China). Absorbance was measured using a microplate reader (Bio-Rad, USA).

Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extra cellular acidiﬁcation rate (ECAR) assay Mitochondrial OCR and ECAR was measured using the Mitochondrial Stress Test Kit (Agilent, USA) and Glycolytic Stress Test Kit (Agilent, USA) with the Seahorse XFe96 analyzer (Seahorse Bioscience, USA), following standard procedures8.

D-glucose-13C6 stable isotope tracer analysis MPC-5 cells were cultured in a glucose-free DMEM medium supplemented with D-glucose-13C6 (4500 mg/L) for 48 hours. After treatment, cells were washed with pre-cooled 0.9% NaCl solution, extracted using methanol at -80 °C, and stored overnight. After vacuum drying, samples were stored at -80 °C for LC-MS analysis. Isotopic tracer analysis was performed using the Lipid ALL method, and 13C metabolites were identiﬁed via high-resolution LC-MS. The relative abundance of metabolites was calculated by normalizing the LC-MS peak intensities. The 13C isotope distribution for each metabolite was determined based on the peak intensities of 13C isotopes.
